own_scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B
own_scenes.desc: Inspirado por el nacionalismo negro de Marcus Garvey («Up you mighty race!»), el Renacimiento de Harlem buscó la sofisticación frente a los estereotipos racistas, con una casta interna (ciudad contra campo, claros contra oscuros) que miraba por encima del hombro el blues rural, es decir, lo funky. Cab Calloway y luego Louis Jordan encarnaron al líder de banda que se mueve al compás y rapea percusivamente. El swing de los treinta, orquestado y estructurado, se alejó de sus raíces hasta que los blancos lo tocaron igual: Benny Goodman y Paul Whiteman se llevaron el dinero, y Ted Vincent lo llama «el disco de los años treinta».

refs.q: The culturally rich “Harlem Renaissance” of the 1920s was a financial and social boon for many blacks
refs.para: The culturally rich “Harlem Renaissance” of the 1920s was a financial and social boon for many blacks who migrated to Harlem and thrived in a lush, urban, yet segregated environment. Black singers, dancers, and musicians stepped in style onstage performing for voyeuristic whites and, after the whites went home, made their own reputations performing for each other, helping to make Harlem the cultural center of the world.

similar_scenes.name: Virginia: Teddy Riley, los Neptunes, Timbaland y Missy Elliott
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: Teddy Riley, arquitecto del new jack swing (hip hop con pop y R&B), se mudó de Nueva York a Virginia Beach y buscó talento en los concursos de los institutos: Pharrell Williams (entonces Magnum the Verb Lord) y Chad Hugo, los Neptunes, coescribieron «Rump Shaker» de Wreckx-n-Effect y luego «Superthug» de Noreaga. Pharrell estuvo en S.B.I. con DJ Timmy Tim (Timbaland) y Magoo; Timbaland conoció a Missy Elliott y acabaron en Da Bassment Crew de DeVanté Swing (Jodeci), encerrados en un sótano sin radio ni tele: por eso inventaron su propio género. Timbaland triunfó con «Pony» de Ginuwine (1996), el One in a Million de Aaliyah y «Up Jumps da Boogie»; Missy, que prefería escribir para otros, sacó Supa Dupa Fly (1997) y allanó el camino de Nicki Minaj, Lizzo o Megan Thee Stallion. En los 2000 parecía que todos los éxitos de la radio los producía alguien de Virginia: sintetizadores, voces moduladas, samples internacionales para Clipse, Jay-Z, Britney Spears o Justin Timberlake.

similar_scenes.name: Naked funk: la era Reagan
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: La era del naked funk abarca las cimas de Prince, Michael Jackson y los dos mandatos de Reagan: recortes, desindustrialización, millones de sin techo, la «guerra contra las drogas» en lugar de contra la pobreza y, desde 1982, el crack. La música negra se volvió narcisista y escapista, del «yo primero»; las bandas, demasiado caras para la ciudad. La industria ofrecía estereotipos (banda pop, crooner, banda funk guarra, según Jon Pareles), MTV no ponía vídeos negros hasta Thriller y Jackson y Prince marcaron las cuotas del crossover. En 1975 trece números 1 R&B eran funk; en 1985 diecisiete de veinte eran baladas. Warner echó a Clinton y CBS sepultó «Pumpin’ It Up»; murieron o se convirtieron Hathaway, Joe Tex, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, Larry Graham. Las máquinas sustituyeron vientos, órgano (el Yamaha DX7), batería y bajo: solo sobrevivió la guitarra rítmica sobre el bajo sintetizado y la palmada electrónica. La insinuación dejó paso al sexo explícito sin cerebro («Do Me Baby», «Beep a Freak»), y llegaron el bass de Miami (2 Live Crew), Egyptian Lover, el New Jack Swing de Teddy Riley y la farsa de Milli Vanilli. Los funkers de verdad abandonaron la radio: el underground (hip hop, go-go) llevó el funk adelante.

similar_scenes.name: Benny Goodman, el rey del swing
similar_scenes.author: Ted Gioia
similar_scenes.desc: La Depresión hunde la venta de discos y el fin de la ley seca desmitifica el jazz, pero la radio en cadena crea el estrellato: managers como Hammond, Glaser o Mills median entre arte y masas. Goodman, hijo de inmigrantes judíos de Maxwell Street y clarinetista de técnica clásica, prepara su triunfo en el programa Let's Dance de la NBC (con arreglos de Fletcher Henderson, «King Porter Stomp», «Sometimes I'm Happy») y estalla en el Palomar Ballroom el 21 de agosto de 1935: nace la era del swing y el fenómeno de fans que anuncia a Sinatra, Elvis o los Beatles. Con Hammond rompe la barrera racial en sus combos (Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton, Charlie Christian), lleva el jazz al Carnegie Hall en 1938 y encarga obras a Bartók, Copland y Hindemith. Gene Krupa populariza al batería como estrella; Bunny Berigan, Harry James, Ziggy Elman, Jess Stacy y luego Mel Powell y Eddie Sauter dan a la banda una modernidad propia, la que el bebop no siguió. Las bandas blancas tuvieron ventajas que Henderson nunca tuvo.

podcast.title: Decline and Transformation (Late 1944)
podcast.body: By the end of 1944, Swing was effectively dead as the dominant popular music form, largely due to a confluence of events including WWII, the ASCAP Boycott, and the Musicians' Union Strike. Swing musicians either transitioned into bebop or began playing new forms of music like Rhythm and Blues, which were inspired by swing but also by boogie and blues. "The end result of all this was that, at the end of 1944, Swing was effectively dead, as was the tradition of instrumentless being the stars in American music."

podcast.title: Dissemination via Radio (WWII Era)
podcast.body: Swing music, as part of a diverse "melting pot" of sounds, was disseminated through radio during World War II. This increased exposure was a consequence of the difficulties Big Bands faced and the American Federation of Musicians strike, which allowed new genres to fill the airwaves. "Boogie-Wooogie, Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, Spear Trolls, a whole new melting pot of sounds was created and disseminated through the radio as a result of the big band problems and the musician's strike."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hi-hat Importance in the 1930s
podcast.body: The sound of hi-hats became a crucial component of the swing and big band era of the 1930s, playing a very important role in the musical style. "The sound of hi-hats became a very important part of the swing and big band-era of the 1930s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Most Popular Music in Mid-1930s North America
podcast.body: By the mid-1930s, swing had become the most popular form of music across North America. The strong emphasis on rhythm, vital for dancing, led to drummers receiving increased attention and respect within the music industry. "By the middle 30s, swing was the most popular form of music in North America, and because such an emphasis was placed on rhythm for dancing, drummers started getting more attention and more respect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Polite Society Reaction
podcast.body: The reaction to Dixieland jazz, from which swing evolved, by polite society in the early 1920s was one of moral panic, similar to later reactions to rock and roll and hip-hop. It was denounced as "evil, jungle music" that incited "ludeness and intoxication" and violence. "It was, in short, everything that was later said about rock and roll, about hip-hop, and you get the idea."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Popularity in the 1930s
podcast.body: Swing music was a dominant and popular genre in the 1930s, serving as the starting point from which Lucky Millinder's band transitioned into the emerging jump band style during the 1940s. "Slowly, during the 1940s, Melinda transitioned his band from the kind of swing music that had been popular in the 30s to the jump band style that was becoming more popular."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Roots in 1920s Jazz
podcast.body: Swing music had its origins in 1920s jazz, but emerged as a distinct form when musicians like Paul Whiteman "cleaned up" the rough edges of earlier jazz, and later solidified with big bands led by figures like Benny Goodman. "Swing was a form of music that had its roots in 1920s jazz."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 1: "Flying Home", Benny Goodman, Charlie Christian, and Lionel Hampton

podcast.title: The Shuffle Rhythm
podcast.body: Swing music is primarily characterized by the shuffle rhythm, where the first beat in a bar is stressed (one and two and three and four). This rhythm was the basis of almost all popular music before the backbeat. While strong and popular, it is described as a "little bit polite, a little bit tame" compared to the excitement of a backbeat. "The shuffle rhythm was the swing rhythm."
